checks.title: One model for every calculation
checks.focus: Margules, first derivative as slope, second derivative as curvature; x ln x endpoint limit; synthetic model.
checks.expected_narration: We will use the symmetric, one-parameter Margules model with A equal to three. This is a synthetic example, not a fitted real-fluid dataset. The first two terms in g describe ideal mixing. The last term describes the excess contribution. The first derivative gives the slope of the curve. The second derivative gives its local curvature. Use natural logarithms in both the energy and the slope. At a pure endpoint, evaluate the limiting value of x times natural log x, which is zero. Keep this model and A fixed while changing the feed in the later comparisons.

checks.title: Step 1: test local curvature
checks.focus: Curvature calculation at z=.12 gives +3.4697 and local stability only; z=.5 gives -2; two-minute pause.
checks.expected_narration: Start with local curvature at z equal to zero point one two. Take one divided by zero point one two, add one divided by zero point eight eight, then subtract six. The result is about positive three point four six nine seven. Positive curvature means sufficiently small composition fluctuations raise the energy, so this homogeneous state is locally stable. It does not exclude a lower-energy split into more distant compositions. At the middle composition, zero point five, the curvature is negative two, so the homogeneous liquid is locally unstable. Pause for two minutes to reproduce both calculations in guide B one.

checks.title: Step 5: calculate the homogeneous energy
checks.expected_narration: Calculate the homogeneous energy term by term. Multiply zero point one two by its natural logarithm. This contributes about negative zero point two five four four three two. The corresponding term for zero point eight eight contributes about negative zero point one one two four nine three. The excess term, three times zero point one two times zero point eight eight, is positive zero point three one six eight. Adding all three gives approximately negative zero point zero five zero one two five. This dimensionless value is total mixing Gibbs energy divided by the number of moles times R T. It is not yet an energy in joules.

checks.title: Step 6: compare with the split
checks.focus: Split g=-.058341, decrease+.008216; metastable homogeneous feed and feasible lower-energy split; total nRT conversion.
checks.expected_narration: Both tangent contacts have the same dimensionless energy, approximately negative zero point zero five eight three four one. Weighting these equal values by phase fractions that add to one gives that same value for the split. Subtract the split energy from the homogeneous energy. The positive decrease is about zero point zero zero eight two one six. The homogeneous feed is therefore metastable: locally stable, but a feasible split lowers the total energy. For an actual total energy decrease, multiply the displayed dimensionless decrease by the total number of moles, R, and the absolute temperature. Pause for five minutes to complete and check guide B three and B four.

checks.title: A different tangent tests the homogeneous feed
checks.focus: Feed tangent TPD versus coexistence common tangent; negative rejects global stability; minimizing trial is not automatically binodal.
checks.expected_narration: Now change the reference line. Tangent-plane distance, or T P D, uses the tangent to the homogeneous curve at the feed composition. At a trial composition w, subtract that feed-tangent value from g of w. A negative result shows that the homogeneous feed is not globally stable. This feed tangent is different from the coexistence common tangent we just verified. Its minimizing trial composition is not automatically a binodal endpoint. In guide C one, keep these two tests distinct: support of the coexistence line verifies the equilibrium construction, while feed T P D tests the original homogeneous liquid.
